introduction_markdown:
**Time allowed: three hours.** This paper contains six questions arranged in three sections: Section A - Physical and General Chemistry (questions 1 and 2); Section B - Inorganic Chemistry (questions 3 and 4); Section C - Organic Chemistry (questions 5 and 6).

Answer ALL the SIX questions in this booklet. The mark allocation is indicated for each question. Each question carries 20 marks. In calculations you are advised to show all the steps in your working, giving your answer at each stage. All necessary working must be shown. No marks will be awarded for answers without brief statements showing how the answers have been obtained. Noiseless calculators may be used.

**Useful data:** $R = 8.314\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}}$ or $0.082\ \mathrm{atm\,dm^3\,K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}}$; one atmosphere (1 atm) = 1 Pa = $1.01\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}$ (as printed); relative atomic masses (RAM): C = 12.0, O = 16.0, S = 32.0, H = 1.0, Cl = 35.5.

questions.enonce_markdown:
This question concerns the elements across period 3 of the periodic table (Na - Ar).

(i) Sketch a graph for the variation of first ionisation energy against atomic number for the elements.

(ii) Complete the table below by giving the chemical formulae of the stable oxides of the elements.

| Element | Na | Mg | P | Cl |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Oxide | | | | |

(iii) Write a balanced equation for the reaction of silicon tetrachloride with water.

(iv) Write two equations to show the amphoteric nature of aluminium oxide ($\mathrm{Al_2O_3}$).

(v) What makes sulphur dioxide gas acidic? *[8 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** Axes: first ionisation energy (vertical) against atomic number 11 to 18, Na to Ar (horizontal). Typical values, $\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$:

| Na | Mg | Al | Si | P | S | Cl | Ar |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 496 | 738 | 578 | 786 | 1012 | 1000 | 1251 | 1521 |

Shape of the graph: a **general upward trend** from sodium (lowest) to argon (highest), because the nuclear charge increases while the electrons are added to the same shell (shielding almost constant), so the atomic radius decreases and the outer electron is held more strongly. There are **two small dips**: at **aluminium** (below magnesium: the 3p electron is higher in energy and slightly shielded by the 3s electrons) and at **sulphur** (below phosphorus: in S one 3p orbital holds a pair of electrons and the repulsion between the paired electrons makes removal easier). Mark Na as the minimum, Ar as the maximum, and show the dips at Al and S.

**(ii)**

| Element | Na | Mg | P | Cl |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Oxide | $\mathrm{Na_2O}$ | $\mathrm{MgO}$ | $\mathrm{P_4O_{10}}$ (or $\mathrm{P_2O_5}$; $\mathrm{P_4O_6}$ is the oxide in limited oxygen) | $\mathrm{Cl_2O_7}$ (oxide of chlorine in its highest oxidation state; $\mathrm{Cl_2O}$ and $\mathrm{ClO_2}$ also exist but are unstable) |

**(iii)** Silicon tetrachloride is completely hydrolysed by water, giving hydrated silicon dioxide (or silicic acid) and fumes of hydrogen chloride:

$\mathrm{SiCl_4(l)} + 2\mathrm{H_2O(l)} \rightarrow \mathrm{SiO_2(s)} + 4\mathrm{HCl(g)}$

(Balance check: Si 1 = 1; Cl 4 = 4; H 4 = 4; O 2 = 2. In excess water the HCl dissolves: $\mathrm{SiCl_4} + 4\mathrm{H_2O} \rightarrow \mathrm{Si(OH)_4} + 4\mathrm{HCl}$.)

**(iv)** Aluminium oxide reacts both with acids (acting as a base) and with bases (acting as an acid):

- With acid: $\mathrm{Al_2O_3(s)} + 6\mathrm{HCl(aq)} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{AlCl_3(aq)} + 3\mathrm{H_2O(l)}$
- With alkali: $\mathrm{Al_2O_3(s)} + 2\mathrm{NaOH(aq)} + 3\mathrm{H_2O(l)} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Na[Al(OH)_4](aq)}$ (sodium tetrahydroxoaluminate; the simplified form is $\mathrm{Al_2O_3} + 2\mathrm{NaOH} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{NaAlO_2} + \mathrm{H_2O}$)

**(v)** Sulphur dioxide is the oxide of a non-metal: it **dissolves in water to form sulphurous acid**, which ionises to give hydrogen ions:

$\mathrm{SO_2(g)} + \mathrm{H_2O(l)} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{H_2SO_3(aq)}$

$\mathrm{H_2SO_3(aq)} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{H^+(aq)} + \mathrm{HSO_3^-(aq)}$

It is the presence of these $\mathrm{H^+}$ ions (the gas also reacts with bases to form sulphites) that makes the solution acidic (pH below 7, turns blue litmus red).

questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) Give the outermost electronic configuration for the s-block elements (group I and group II).

(ii) For the elements lithium and beryllium, write equations representing:

A: First ionization energy for Lithium.

B: Second ionization energy for Beryllium.

(iii) Which of these two elements in b(ii) will have a higher second ionization energy? Explain. *[5 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** Group I: $ns^1$ (one electron in the outer s orbital, e.g. $2s^1$ for Li). Group II: $ns^2$ (e.g. $2s^2$ for Be), where $n$ is the period number (the principal quantum number of the outermost shell).

**(ii)** State symbols are required:

- **A:** $\mathrm{Li(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{Li^+(g)} + e^-$
- **B:** $\mathrm{Be^+(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{Be^{2+}(g)} + e^-$

**(iii) Lithium** has the higher second ionisation energy (about 7298 against 1757 $\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ for beryllium).

Explanation: the second ionisation of lithium removes an electron from $\mathrm{Li^+}$, which has the stable noble-gas configuration $1s^2$; this electron is in the **inner shell, much closer to the nucleus and much less shielded**, so it is held very strongly. The second ionisation of beryllium removes the remaining $2s$ electron from $\mathrm{Be^+}$ ($1s^2 2s^1$), an electron in the **outer shell**, further from the nucleus and shielded by the $1s^2$ electrons, so much less energy is needed.

questions.enonce_markdown:
The halogens are the elements in group VII of the periodic table (F, Cl, Br, I).

(i) Complete the table by giving the colour of each element.

| Element | $\mathrm{F_2}$ | $\mathrm{Cl_2}$ | $\mathrm{Br_2}$ | $\mathrm{I_2}$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Colour | | | | |

(ii) Account for the change in physical state (if any) for the elements. *[5 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)**

| Element | $\mathrm{F_2}$ | $\mathrm{Cl_2}$ | $\mathrm{Br_2}$ | $\mathrm{I_2}$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Colour | pale yellow | yellow-green (greenish-yellow) | red-brown (orange-brown vapour) | grey-black solid (violet vapour) |

**(ii)** At room temperature the physical state changes down the group: **fluorine and chlorine are gases, bromine is a liquid, iodine is a solid** (the melting and boiling points increase down the group).

Reason: the halogens exist as **simple diatomic molecules** held together in the solid and liquid by weak **van der Waals (instantaneous dipole-induced dipole, London) forces**. Going down the group, the molecules contain **more electrons and are larger**, so they are more polarisable and the van der Waals forces between molecules become stronger. More energy is needed to separate the molecules, so the melting and boiling points rise and the state changes from gas to liquid to solid.

questions.enonce_markdown:
The hydrogen halides are HF, HCl, HBr and HI.

In the space provided sketch a graph of boiling point against relative molecular mass for the halides.

Explain the shape of the graph. *[3 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Sketch.** Axes: boiling point (vertical) against relative molecular mass (horizontal): HF 20, HCl 36.5, HBr 81, HI 128. Approximate boiling points: HF about $+20\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$ (293 K), HCl about $-85\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$, HBr about $-67\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$, HI about $-35\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

Shape: HF is plotted **high** (anomalously high boiling point, well above HCl); then HCl is the **lowest** point and the curve **rises steadily** through HBr to HI.

**Explanation.**

- **HF** has an abnormally high boiling point because fluorine is very small and the most electronegative element, so the molecules form strong **hydrogen bonds** ($\mathrm{H{-}F \cdots H{-}F}$) in addition to van der Waals forces; much more energy is needed to separate them.
- From **HCl to HI** there is no hydrogen bonding (Cl, Br and I are larger and less electronegative). The molecules are held by van der Waals forces (and permanent dipole-dipole attractions), which **increase as the relative molecular mass and the number of electrons increase**, so the boiling point rises from HCl to HBr to HI.
